title: After Kalki, the wheel turns
hookLine: after Kalki, the Bhagavata's new age starts with a scent on the wind
carry: time is a wheel: the age of truth returns
tomorrow: someone online calls an old law book 'the Hindu rulebook.' is it?
last: A HARD AGE, ONE DOOR OPEN.

cards: When a long guest leaves, a house smells different for a while: their shampoo in the bathroom, their snack in the pantry, and then, slowly, just home again. A smell can be the first thing that says a season has turned.
In the Bhagavata, that's how the next age begins. Not with a trumpet, but with a scent on the wind.
Once Kalki has done his work, a breeze moves across the earth carrying sandalwood, and the people who breathe it find their minds gone clear.

teach.h: A BREEZE WITH SANDALWOOD IN IT.

teach.b: When Kalki has put down the robbers who ruled as kings, the people who remain are touched by a breeze carrying the fragrance of sandal paste from the Lord's own body, and their minds turn clear.

teach.h: THE AGE OF TRUTH BEGINS AGAIN.
teach.b: Then the Krita age, the age of truth, begins again. The book even mentions two kings who have been waiting quietly in a village called Kalapa, ready to start the royal lines over. So Kalki isn't the end of the story.
He's the hinge that swings the ages back to the start: Krita, Treta, Dvapara, Kali, and then Krita once more.

teach.h: FOUR YUGAS: A WHEEL, NOT AN ARROW.
teach.b: These are the four yugas, and this is a core Hindu picture of time: it turns like a wheel, not an arrow, and an ending is also the place where something starts.

teach.h: THE WHOLE SERIES, LOOKED BACK ON.
teach.b: Now step back and see the whole series these weeks have walked. A fish in the flood. A tortoise under the mountain.
A boar lifting the earth. A man-lion at the doorway. A dwarf's strides.
Rama with the axe, and Rama with the bow. Krishna. The Buddha, as the tradition tells him.
And Kalki, still to come, opening the wheel's next turn. Age after age, Krishna said in the Gita; the ten forms are that line, told as a story. The weeks in the Puranas close here.
Next comes a different kind of book, a dharma text, read with care and a critical eye.

how: Sandal paste is offered in Hindu worship and applied to images of the gods; the four ages and their turning are retold in Purana recitations.

o: the one whose work turns the ages back to truth
the breeze that carries sandalwood over the earth
a king waiting in Kalapa to restart a royal line

p: the age of truth, begun again

s: in the Bhagavata, the new age after Kalki begins with a battle cry
it begins with a breeze carrying sandal fragrance, and minds turn clear.
the Bhagavata mentions kings waiting in a village to restart the royal lines

games.q: your cousin asks which line from the Gita the ten forms tell as a story. which one fits?
o: I come age after age, whenever dharma slips.
you have the right to the work, not to its fruit.
but Krishna is the Lord himself.
games.why: yuge yuge, age after age: the fish, the boar, the man-lion and the rest, down to Kalki still to come, are that line told as a story.

practice: Sandal paste is offered to the gods in puja, and any scent will do for this. If there's something with a scent near you, a spice jar, soap, a cup of tea, hold it close and breathe it in slowly, three times.
Then set it down and keep breathing in the trace it leaves. If there's nothing nearby, notice the plain smell of the room.

wordCard.voice: Kalki: the form whose work closes the Kali age, after which a sandal-scented breeze clears minds and the age of truth comes round again.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the Krita age, the age of truth, which comes round again after Kalki.

carryVoice: Keep this: time is a wheel, and the age of truth returns. Kalki is the hinge where it turns. And with that, the Puranas are done.
